title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. Execution used the declared model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) under shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one initial LLM generation per task, reused across arms); the guarded pipeline could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. We ran N=240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial). All archived final outcomes were scored as safe under both arms (baseline_safe = 240/240; guarded_safe = 240/240). The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate contract the paired contrast is only informative when the shared initial candidate fails deterministic validation or when a validator‑triggered repair changes the final configuration; in this run all shared candidates passed validation and no repairs were invoked, producing a degenerate paired outcome. We report the preregistered design, execution accounting, artifact‑grounded analysis, a mechanistic failure analysis for the null paired contrast, and concrete recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction: Translating high‑level operator intent into safe device configurations is a central NetOps task. Large language models (LLMs) and emergent agentic patterns can generate multi‑step configuration sequences, but textual similarity metrics fail to capture ordering, dependency, and invariants required for safe application to network devices. Emulation‑grounded evaluation—executing generated configs in deterministic emulators or device images and checking semantic invariants—reveals operational failure modes (ordering violations, transient safety breaches, protected‑resource touches) that text‑only tests miss. A common engineering pattern is generate–validate–repair (GVR): an LLM generates a candidate, a deterministic verifier checks semantic invariants, and a repair routine rewrites candidates that violate constraints. Prior work documents this pattern in program/configuration repair prototypes and emulation benchmarks, but experimental questions remain about when deterministic verifiers measurably reduce unsafe applications under realistic distribution shift and adversarial prompts. Our preregistered paired experiment was designed to measure a single estimand precisely: the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded minus baseline), under shared_initial_candidate generation semantics. We focus on emulation‑grounded, artifact‑traceable measurement and on explaining the operational meaning of the observed null paired contrast.
sections.related_work: Executable, closed‑loop NetOps benchmarks that exercise planning and execution faults have recently appeared; such benchmarks motivate emulation‑grounded evaluation of agentic LLM pipelines [1]. Generate–validate architectures appear across configuration repair and program‑repair literature and often improve syntactic and many semantic failure modes when validators have sufficient coverage [2], [3]. Surveys of agentic evaluation and LLM‑for‑NetOps position papers emphasize tool augmentation, verifier integration, and uncertainty gating as architectural levers for operational safety [4], [5]. Work on configuration analysis tools (engineering predecessors such as Batfish) and recent emulation benchmarks provide practical patterns for deterministic checking and incremental verification [6]. Our study differs by preregistering a paired estimand with shared_initial_candidate semantics, executing an emulation‑grounded paired run, and publishing artifact‑grounded analysis that explains why the guarded intervention did or did not produce discordant paired outcomes.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand: We preregistered the study (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01). The primary estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, defined as the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline) where unsafe_apply = 1 indicates a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation when applied. Design and generation semantics: The experiment used paired episodes with shared_initial_candidate semantics: the adapter produced one initial LLM candidate per task and that same candidate was used by both arms; the guarded arm could request up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. This contract makes the paired contrast conditional on the shared candidate failing validation or on a repair changing the final output. Sampling and tasks: N = 240 distinct intent→configuration tasks were executed, blocked as 144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift (novel topologies/vendors), and 48 adversarial‑prompt items (adversarial prompts generated under a preregistered adversary protocol). Model and tooling: Execution used the declared model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) as the semantic oracle; an orchestration adapter implemented the GVR contract. Budget and operational constraints: the adapter contract limited generation to one shared initial generation per task and allowed at most one repair call per guarded episode; model calls and verifier calls were recorded in the archived execution manifest. Scoring and analysis mapping: The deterministic scorer produced a binary final outcome (safe vs unsafe) per episode based on emulator execution and explicit invariant checks. The primary analysis used a paired contingency estimator with exact McNemar test and bootstrap percentile CIs (10,000 resamples); analysis parameters (resample count and seed) were preregistered and the analysis executor recorded them.
sections.results: Execution accounting: The run completed per the preregistered plan. Exactly 240 paired tasks were executed; planned episodes = 480 and completed episodes = 480. The adapter produced exactly one shared initial generation per task (one model generation per pair under the registered contract). Primary binary outcomes: Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms. Aggregate counts: baseline_safe = 240/240, guarded_safe = 240/240. Paired contingency: n11 (both safe) = 240; n10 (guarded safe, baseline unsafe) = 0; n01 (guarded unsafe, baseline safe) = 0; n00 (both unsafe) = 0. Estimation and inference: the paired estimator (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729). McNemar exact two‑sided p = 1.0. Validator and repair activity: no validator‑triggered repairs were applied during the run; all shared initial candidates passed deterministic validation, so the guarded pipeline had no repair events to exercise. Subgroup slices (in‑distribution, shift, adversarial) are degenerate: all subgroups show zero unsafe applies in both arms.
sections.discussion: Mechanistic explanation for the null paired contrast: Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics a single LLM candidate was shared by both arms; the guarded arm can only change the paired outcome by (a) the shared candidate failing deterministic validation and triggering a repair, or (b) the guard invoking a repair even when the shared candidate nominally passed (not permitted under the contract). In this run every shared candidate passed the deterministic checks and repair budget usage was zero; therefore no generator/validator interaction could create discordant paired outcomes and the paired contrast is degenerate. Design implications: shared_initial_candidate semantics reduce model‑call cost and produce direct pairing of generator output, but they also make the causal contrast contingent on generator failures. To obtain informative paired estimates of verifier benefit, experiments should (i) allow independent initial generations per arm to introduce generator variability, or (ii) increase adversary strength so that shared candidates are more likely to violate verifier constraints, or (iii) expand the repair budget so repair behaviour can be exercised when validation fails. Threats to validity: internal validity is affected by the shared_initial_candidate contract (explicit design choice); construct validity depends on deterministic validator coverage (finite check set may miss semantic fault classes); external validity is limited by the emulation corpus and synthetic task generator; conclusion validity is constrained by realized baseline unsafe rate = 0, which precludes detection of positive verifier effects under the chosen contract. Recommendations for future GVR evaluations: avoid shared_initial_candidate when the scientific goal is to measure verifier causal effect, instrument and allow richer repair searches, broaden adversary protocols to probe adaptive manipulations, and extend validator semantic coverage with cross‑checks between validator PASS and emulator execution outcomes.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a generate–validate–repair pipeline for intent→configuration translation. Observed outcome: all 240 paired tasks were scored safe under both the LLM‑only baseline and the guarded GVR arm; the paired difference = 0.00 (95% CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). The null paired contrast is explained mechanistically by the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics combined with a deterministic validator that passed every shared candidate; because no repairs were invoked the guarded arm could not produce discordant paired outcomes. The archived experiment artifacts and analysis parameters substantiate these facts and support concrete design changes (independent generation per arm, larger repair budgets, stronger adversaries, and expanded verifier coverage) required for informative future paired tests of verifier effectiveness. Full execution and analysis artifacts are archived in the study bundle and available for inspection per the reproducibility statement below. References are provided in conventional IEEE format in the manuscript bibliography below.

limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a synthetic, emulation‑grounded corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini) and one validator implementation were tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompts, validator designs, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design reused one initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.

Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite set of semantic checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected and could produce false‑safe outcomes in other settings.
